overview: The Medford Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) adjudicates requests for dimensional relief, special permits, and variances for residential and commercial developments in the city. The board frequently reviews projects ranging from simple home additions and fence heights to major Chapter 40B multi-family housing developments and commercial use conversions. Over the course of the meetings from mid-2024 through late 2026, the board has transitioned its leadership and integrated new state regulations regarding accessory dwelling units into its deliberations. At its most recent meeting, the board focused on navigating state-level zoning changes while managing several pending residential petitions.

threads.name: Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs)
threads.summary: The board began specifically addressing ADUs in late 2026 following changes to state zoning regulations. While a variance for an attached ADU on Fulton Street was approved in July 2026, other petitions on Vassar Street and Wellesley Street were continued to allow for city legal counsel to review the new state standards. By September 2024, these cases remained pending as the board sought modified designs and further legal clarification on state guidelines.

threads.name: Flood Mitigation and Topographical Hardships
threads.summary: The board often grants variances to address property-specific hardships caused by flooding or unusual lot shapes. In 2024, it approved parking and setback variances on Lincoln Street and Judkins Road specifically to facilitate drainage improvements and flood prevention. Similar relief was granted for properties with diagonal orientations or narrow footprints on Winchester Road and Monument Street to allow for code-compliant renovations.

threads.name: Commercial-to-Residential Conversions
threads.summary: The board regularly reviews petitions to convert underutilized commercial spaces into housing. This includes the approved conversion of a first-floor unit on Main Street into a residential unit and the demolition of a motor vehicle repair station on Elm Street to build a three-unit townhouse. In mid-2026, the board also approved the conversion of a non-conforming single-family dwelling into a two-family structure on Main Street.

threads.name: Administrative Reform and Backlog Management
threads.summary: Beginning in July 2024, the board identified a need to update its dated rules and regulations, eventually appointing a subcommittee for the task. To address a persistent backlog of meeting minutes, staff reported in early 2025 that they were testing AI software to assist with drafting records. By late 2025, this technology was being utilized to help the board catch up on its administrative requirements.

threads.name: Cannabis Operations
threads.summary: The board managed zoning relief for local cannabis dispensaries. In June 2026, a hearing for delivery services at 114 Mystic Avenue was continued to await legal counsel. The board subsequently approved the special permit for those delivery services in July 2026.

threads.name: Chapter 40B and Major Developments
threads.summary: The board oversees high-density projects under Chapter 40B, though some applicants choose to withdraw, such as a 378-unit proposal on Mystic Avenue in June 2024. For existing approvals, like the 350-unit development at 4000 Mystic Valley Parkway, the board reviews design refinements to determine if they constitute substantial changes. It also facilitates lot splits for larger commercial structures to allow for adjacent residential projects, as seen with the Fellsway project in early 2025.

threads.name: Board Leadership and Membership
threads.summary: The board underwent a leadership transition in early 2025 following the resignation of Chair Jamie Thompson. Mike Caldera was elected as the new chair in February 2025. During this period, the board also coordinated with the Mayor's office regarding the appointment of new members to fill vacancies and ensure a quorum.

periods.narrative: This period was characterized by a high volume of residential relief requests for additions and a focus on resolving administrative backlogs using new software.
The board began navigating new state mandates regarding accessory dwelling units and handled several high-profile use conversions from commercial to residential or service-oriented businesses.
